title: Critical AI capability, active exploitation and control evidence now meet in one operating test
mainJudgement: The test is simple: when a warning lands, can the firm turn it into a clear, evidenced decision?

committeeQuestion.question: For the risks we say are critical—agentic AI, exploited vulnerabilities, sanctions change and data failure—can management show the trigger, intervention authority, evidence of action and closure decision?
committeeQuestion.why: This week’s signals are different in form but identical in management demand: speed matters only when the firm can recognise the trigger, act within authority and preserve a decision trail that survives challenge.
committeeQuestion.evidence: Ask for one recent end-to-end example: the alert or evaluation, named owner, authority to intervene, control action, exception decision, recovery or remediation proof, and dated closure record.

committeeQuestions.question: For one important AI-enabled workflow, who can stop or change it—and can management show that authority works?
committeeQuestions.why: As systems move from assisting people to taking action, the practical control is not a policy. It is a named person, a real permission boundary and a route that works under pressure.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The workflow, its permissions, the named intervention authority, the stop or rollback route and one recent test or decision record.

committeeQuestions.question: Which important customer services would fail together if a shared cloud, identity, data or model provider were impaired—and when did we last test the fallback?
committeeQuestions.why: Individual supplier assessments can miss a common dependency. A disruption becomes the firm’s problem when multiple important services depend on the same underlying provider or control plane.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The service-and-dependency map, common points of failure, impact tolerance, fallback plan, test result and accountable owner.

committeeQuestions.question: Can management trace one recent cyber or data issue from alert to closure, including the decision, action, exception and proof that the fix worked?
committeeQuestions.why: Seeing an alert is not the same as controlling the risk. The committee needs confidence that an issue can be identified, owned, remedied and closed with evidence that survives scrutiny.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The original alert, named owner, decision log, remediation record, any accepted exception, retest result and dated closure record.

judgement.observation: This week’s AI, cyber, sanctions and data events all point to one management test: when a warning lands, can the firm turn it into a clear, evidenced decision?
judgement.executiveJudgement: The weakness is rarely seeing the alert. It is being able to show who could act, what they decided and whether the issue was closed properly. A policy or dashboard alone cannot do that.
judgement.implication: Pick two critical scenarios and trace the evidence from trigger to closure. Start with an exploited vulnerability and a sanctions change. Name the owner, their authority, the action taken and the proof it worked.
